report:
Conclusion: No. The best evidence does not show that hydroxychloroquine reduces the likelihood of dying from COVID-19. Large randomized trials and syntheses found no mortality benefit, and regulators withdrew emergency authorization because effectiveness was unlikely and cardiac risks were known.

The U.K. RECOVERY randomized comparison—1,542 patients assigned hydroxychloroquine versus 3,132 assigned usual care—was stopped after finding no survival benefit; subsequent summaries of randomized evidence reached the same conclusion (https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/factcheck/2020/07/21/fact-check-hydroxychloroquine-hasnt-helped-covid-19-studies-show/5407547002/). A systematic review/meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials specifically examining mortality and viral clearance likewise found no clear mortality reduction (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8220439/). Oxford’s evidence review concluded early positive signals were weak/flawed and later higher-quality trials did not support benefit, with some studies suggesting worse outcomes or serious side effects (https://www.cebm.net/covid-19/chloroquine-and-hydroxychloroquine-current-evidence-for-their-effectiveness-in-treating-covid-19/). On June 15, 2020, the FDA revoked the emergency use authorization for chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine, stating the drugs were unlikely to be effective and that known/potential risks outweighed unproven benefits (https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/coronavirus-covid-19-update-fda-revokes-emergency-use-authorization-chloroquine-and).

Bottom line: hydroxychloroquine should not be used to reduce COVID-19 death risk outside approved indications; evidence-based COVID-19 care should follow current clinical guidance.
